passages.original: inspectum uolnus absterso cruore; omnia salubria esse; confidere propediem ipsum eos uisuros; interim Ser.Tullio iubere populum dicto audientem esse; eum iura redditurum obiturumque alia regis munia esse. Seruius cum trabea et lictoribus prodit ac sede regia sedens alia decernit, de aliis consulturum se regem esse simulat. itaque per aliquot dies cum iam exspirasset Tarquinius celata morte per speciem alienae fungendae uicis suas opes firmauit;
passages.english: the wound had been examined after the blood was wiped away; all the signs were healthy; she was confident that they would see the king himself very soon; meanwhile he ordered the people to obey Servius Tullius; he would administer justice and perform the king's other duties. Servius came out wearing the *trabea* [the royal striped robe] and attended by lictors, and sitting on the royal seat he decided some matters, and on others he pretended that he would consult the king. And so for several days, though Tarquinius had already died, with the death concealed, under the pretence of acting as another's deputy he strengthened his own power;
passages.notes: The passage continues the indirect speech of Tanaquil from the preceding context; 'iubere' (he ordered) refers to the king's supposed command.

passages.original: a quo facessere iussa ex tanto tumultu cum se domum reciperet peruenissetque ad summum Cyprium uicum, ubi Dianium nuper fuit, flectenti carpentum dextra in Urbium cliuum ut in collem Esquiliarum eueheretur, restitit pauidus atque inhibuit frenos is qui iumenta agebat iacentemque dominae Seruium trucidatum ostendit. foedum inhumanumque inde traditur scelus monumentoque locus est—Sceleratum uicum uocant—quo amens, agitantibus furiis sororis ac uiri, Tullia per patris corpus carpentum egisse fertur, partemque sanguinis ac caedis paternae cruento uehiculo, contaminata ipsa respersaque, tulisse ad penates suos uirique sui, quibus iratis malo regni principio similes propediem exitus sequerentur.
passages.english: Ordered by him to leave such a scene of uproar, as she was returning home and had reached the top of the Cyprian Street, where the shrine of Diana stood until recently, as she was turning her carriage to the right onto the Urbian Slope to drive up to the Esquiline hill, the man who was driving the animals stopped in terror, pulled up the reins, and showed his mistress Servius lying murdered. A foul and inhuman crime is reported to have followed, and the place serves as a memorial of it—they call it the Street of Crime—where Tullia, out of her mind, driven by the avenging spirits of her sister and her husband, is said to have driven her carriage over her father's body, and, herself defiled and spattered, to have carried part of her father's blood and slaughter on the bloodstained vehicle to her own household gods and her husband's; and in their anger, an end like the evil beginning of the reign was soon to follow.
passages.notes: 'Furiis' may mean the Furies or the avenging ghosts of her murdered sister and first husband; rendered as 'avenging spirits'.
